lesson.title: Sideways Overlap: Pi Bonds and Why Double Bonds Are Flat
lesson.summary: A pi bond forms from the sideways overlap of two leftover, unhybridized p orbitals above and below the bond axis, and it is what locks double and triple bonds into rigid, non-rotating shapes.
lesson.body:
A pi, or π, bond forms very differently from a sigma bond. Instead of two orbitals meeting head on along the internuclear axis, a pi bond forms when two unhybridized p orbitals, both lying parallel to each other and both perpendicular to the sigma bond axis, overlap side by side. This sideways overlap produces two separate regions of electron density, one lobe above the plane of the sigma bond and one lobe below it, rather than one continuous region wrapped around the axis the way a sigma bond has.

Pi bonds never appear on their own. A pi bond always forms in addition to a sigma bond that already connects the same two atoms, never as a replacement for it, which is why a double bond is described as one sigma bond plus one pi bond, and a triple bond as one sigma bond plus two pi bonds. Forming a pi bond also requires a leftover, unhybridized p orbital on each atom involved, which immediately connects back to hybridization: sp2 hybridized atoms have exactly one leftover p orbital and so can form one pi bond, sp hybridized atoms have two leftover p orbitals and so can form two pi bonds, and sp3 hybridized atoms have no leftover p orbitals at all and therefore cannot form any pi bonds.

Ethylene, C2H4, shows a double bond built this way. Each carbon is sp2 hybridized, and the sp2 orbitals on the two carbons overlap head on to form the C-C sigma bond, exactly as described for sigma bonds. Each carbon also has one leftover p orbital standing perpendicular to the plane of the molecule. Those two p orbitals, one on each carbon, overlap sideways with each other to form the pi bond, and together the sigma bond and the pi bond make up the full C=C double bond.

A triple bond simply adds a second pi bond using a second pair of leftover p orbitals. In acetylene, C2H2, each sp hybridized carbon has two unhybridized p orbitals, oriented perpendicular to each other. One pair of p orbitals, one from each carbon, overlaps sideways to form one pi bond, and the other pair overlaps sideways to form a second pi bond at right angles to the first, giving the carbon-carbon triple bond its one sigma plus two pi bond structure. Nitrogen gas, N2, follows the same pattern between its two sp hybridized nitrogen atoms.

The side by side geometry of a pi bond has an important consequence that sigma bonds do not share: rotating one end of the molecule around the bond axis would pull the two parallel p orbitals out of alignment and break the overlap that holds the pi bond together. That is why double and triple bonds resist rotation and hold the atoms attached to them in a fixed, rigid, planar arrangement, in sharp contrast to the free rotation possible around a pure sigma bond like the one in ethane. This rigidity is also the reason molecules built around a C=C double bond can exist as distinct cis and trans forms that do not freely interconvert.
